1:1:
Title: ΕΥΑΓΓΕΛΙΟΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΜΑΘΘΑΙΟΝ. εὐαγγέλιον, in earlier Greek, signified a present made as a return for good news, or a thank-offering for the same; in later Greek (LXX, and N.T. passim), the good news itself — here, the good news of salvation by Christ Jesus. Hence it came to be applied to the writings which contain this good news (so already Justin Martyr, Apol. i. 66).

κατὰ Μαθθαῖον = as delivered by (i.e. on the authority and editorship of) Matthew: compare Ὅμηρος κατὰ Ἀρίσταρχον. It is not a mere genitive of authorship (which would have been τὸ εὐαγγέλιον αὐτοῦ), nor does it imply that the teaching only, and not the written Gospel, was Matthew's: see Eusebius, H.E. iii. 24.

vv. 1–17. The Genealogy. 1. βίβλος γενέσεως is not the title of the whole Gospel, but, as is plain from the limits of the genealogy itself (it is not always used of a pedigree only, but here it refers exclusively to the genealogy), since Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ is used in the opening clause and the close is Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεγόμενος χριστός; ver. 17 then forms the conclusion, and ver. 18 passes to other matter.

υἱοῦ Δαυείδ, υἱοῦ Ἀβραάμ — both refer to our Lord. 'Son of David' was an especial title of the Messiah (see reff.): that He should also be Son of Abraham was too solemn a subject of prophecy to be omitted, even though implied in the former. As Euthymius observes, nothing so reassured the believing Jews as to learn that the Christ was of the seed of Abraham and of David. Luke (iii. 23 ff.) carries the genealogy further back, to Adam.

χριστοῦ = Heb. māshîach, anointed: used in the O.T. of kings, priests, and prophets, and of the promised Deliverer; here used (as in ver. 16) in the sense in which it became affixed to the name of our Lord as a proper title.
1:2: 2. καὶ τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς αὐτοῦ — this addition (with the similar one at ver. 11) probably indicates that Matthew did not simply copy his genealogy from a family register, but constructed it with a purpose: 'Obiter Matthæus Christum ut cognatum omnibus Israelitis commendat' (Grotius).
1:3: 3. The children of Judah by Tamar were not born in lawful marriage (Gen. xxxviii. 16–30); both sons are named, probably to recall the incident of their birth. The mention of the four women in this genealogy (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba) has been variously explained: Wetstein thinks it meets a tacit Jewish objection; Fritzsche, that it is for the sake of exactness; most probably, with Maldonatus, the Evangelist passes over what was ordinary and notes what was singular and questionable in the descent. De Wette adds that these women may also serve as types of the mother of our Lord, named, like them, in the course of an otherwise male genealogy.
1:5: 5. Ῥαχάβ — the use of the article (τῆς Ῥαχάβ) and its relative force confirm that this is indeed Rahab of Jericho (so Bengel), against those who on chronological grounds have doubted the identification. The chronology in fact agrees well enough: Naashon, father of Salmon, was a prince of Judah at the setting up of the tabernacle, thirty-nine years before the fall of Jericho, so that Salmon would be of full age when Rahab — whose parents were then still living — was probably young. The longer interval sometimes alleged between Rahab and David belongs equally to the genealogy in Ruth iv. 21, 22, and is not insuperable in view of the great age of Jesse implied in 1 Sam. xvii. 12.
1:6: 6. τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου — 'her that had been the wife of Uriah': a construction not properly elliptical but possessive, as in Ἕκτορος Ἀνδρομάχη, occurring elsewhere in the Gospels to designate various relations.
1:8: 8, 9, 10. Three kings — Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah (cf. 1 Chron. iii. 11, 12) — are silently omitted between Joram and Ozias. Some (Spanheim, Lightfoot, Ebrard) suppose they were struck out of the royal line on account of their connexion, through Athaliah, with the accursed house of Ahab — comparable to the omission of Simeon in Moses' blessing (Deut. xxxiii.), or of Dan from the tribes sealed in Rev. vii. More probably, whatever the original ground, the omission here serves the simpler purpose of squaring the numbers of the genealogy into the three equal divisions of ver. 17 (cf. similarly 1 Chron. viii. 1 with Gen. xlvi. 21).
1:11: 11. Ἰωσείας ἐγέννησεν τὸν Ἰεχονίαν — Eliakim (Jehoiakim), son of Josiah and father of Jechonias, is here passed over. This was objected to the Christians by Porphyry. The reading inserting Joacim is very weakly supported, and would in any case overfill the second tessaradecade. The true solution probably lies, as Lord A. Hervey argues at length, in some recognized Jewish manner of reckoning Eliakim and his son together as it were one link — comparable to the way 2 Chron. xxxvi. 10 calls Zedekiah (really Jechonias's uncle) his 'brother.'
1:12:
12. ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας = at the time of the migration to Babylon (a use of ἐπί with the genitive akin to its local sense of 'upon, at the point of'); μετὰ τὴν μετοικεσίαν = after the migration.

Ἰεχονίας... Σαλαθιήλ — so also 1 Chron. iii. 17. The prophecy that Jeconiah should be 'childless' (Jer. xxii. 30) is explained by the rest of that verse: no descendant of his was to prosper upon David's throne — not that he should have no offspring at all.

Σαλαθιήλ... Ζοροβάβελ — no greater difficulty here than already exists within the O.T. itself, where Zerubbabel is elsewhere called son of Shealtiel (Ezra iii. 2; Hag. i. 1) yet also son of Pedaiah, Shealtiel's brother (1 Chron. iii. 19) — explained either by a different Zerubbabel, or, more probably, by a levirate raising-up of seed.
1:13: 13. Ζοροβάβελ... Ἀβιούδ — Abiud does not appear as a son of Zerubbabel in 1 Chron. iii.; Lord A. Hervey has made it probable that Abiud is identical with the Hodaiah of 1 Chron. iii. 24, and with the Juda of Luke iii. 26 — a conjecture not adopted by all, but a careful and reverent attempt to reconcile the two genealogies, well worth the student's attention.
1:16: 16. Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας, ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεγόμενος χριστός — the genealogy is throughout traced through Joseph (necessarily, as he was the legal head of the family), but at this last link the strict ἐγέννησεν is deliberately broken: Joseph is named as the husband of Mary, and it is of her that Jesus was born — a construction which, taken with ver. 18 ff., guards from the outset against any inference that Joseph was His natural father.
1:17:
17. γενεαὶ δεκατέσσαρες (three times) — observing Matthew's arrangement carefully removes the apparent difficulty. The first tessaradecade runs from Abraham to David inclusive; the second from David (again inclusive) to the migration, with Jechonias — whose begetting coincides with the migration itself — reserved for the third; the third then runs from Jechonias to Christ inclusive. It is not necessary, with Meyer, to suppose that Matthew imagined this scheme to be a complete record of every generation and was simply ignorant of the omissions (cf. on ver. 11): he may, for his readers' convenience, have deliberately cast a genealogy he knew to be selective into this memorable threefold, fourteen-generation form.

vv. 18–25. Circumstances of the Birth of Christ. 18. τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ — the combined name is put first emphatically, resuming the subject of ver. 1.

γένεσις (not γέννησις, which crept in here from ver. 16) is to be understood in the wide sense of 'origin,' nearly = γέννησις, but probably chosen by the Holy Spirit to mark a slight distinction between the γένεσις of our Lord and the ordinary γέννησις of other men.

μνηστευθείσης — the interval between betrothal and the consummation of marriage was sometimes considerable, the betrothed meanwhile remaining in her father's house until the bridegroom came to fetch her (cf. Deut. xx. 7).

[γὰρ] is explicative ('seeing that it was thus...'), or possibly apologetic for the οὕτως, explaining that an account of so unusual a circumstance was needed.

συνελθεῖν = to come together as man and wife under one roof — the deductio in domum mariti — corresponding to παραλαβεῖν in vv. 20, 24.
1:19:
19. δίκαιος ὤν — a strict observer of the law; καὶ μὴ θέλων is not, as the μή plainly shews, an explanation of δίκαιος but an additional and distinct trait: he was just, and (yet, or and withal) unwilling to expose her. The sense 'kind' or 'merciful' for δίκαιος is inadmissible here.

λάθρα ἀπολῦσαι — not without any bill of divorcement (which would have been unlawful), but quietly, according to the form prescribed in Deut. xxiv. 1, rather than by the harsher public process which, under Deut. xxii. 23, could have ended in the woman's death by stoning.

ἐβουλήθη — denotes intention, the wish ripened into resolve, as distinct from θέλω, the mere wish (see Buttmann's Lexilogus).
1:20:
20. ἰδού answers to the Hebrew, and is used by Matthew and Luke (less often by Mark, never thus by John) to introduce a new event or change of scene.

The announcement was made to Mary openly but to Joseph only in a dream, since in Mary's case faith and the concurrence of her will were required, and the communication was of a higher kind; here it is simply a caution, after the fact, regarding what had already happened.

υἱὸς Δαυείδ — this form of address would recall to Joseph's mind the promised seed and the hope of his lineage, and at once mark the message as the announcement of the Messiah's birth.

τὴν γυναῖκά σου — not predicative ('as thy wife') but in apposition with Μαριάμ — 'Mary, thy wife' — reminding Joseph of the relation she already held to him by betrothal, which he is now exhorted to acknowledge fully (cf. ver. 24).
1:21:
21. Ἰησοῦν = the same name as Joshua, the former deliverer of Israel; Philo explains Ἰησοῦς as 'salvation of the Lord.'

αὐτὸς is emphatic: He, and He alone, shall save.

τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ (not αὐτῶν) — primarily the Jews, the only sense Joseph could yet have grasped; but in the larger sense, all who believe on Him, a sense warranted by the tenor of prophecy (Gen. xxii. 18; Deut. xxxii. 21) and the subsequent admission of the Gentiles.

ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν — a remarkably clear early indication, amid the pedigrees and political expectations surrounding a 'King of the Jews,' of the truly spiritual nature of Christ's office; ἁμαρτία here is the practice of sin itself, not merely its punishment. As Bishop Ellicott observes, it is suggestive that while to the loftier spirit of Mary the name is revealed with all the prophetic associations of David's glory, to Joseph — perhaps already alive to his own and others' spiritual need — it is simply said: He shall save His people from their sins.
1:22:
22. τοῦτο δὲ ὅλον... ἵνα πληρωθῇ — ἵνα cannot, on N.T. usage, mean anything but 'in order that': the fulfilment of a formally given promise may rightly be cited as the final cause of an event that exceeds, and was purposed long before, the original utterance.

The immediate, literal fulfilment of Isaiah's prophecy belongs to the time of Ahaz (Isa. viii. 1–4); but already within that same context (viii. 8) the name 'Emmanuel' is applied to one of greater dignity, and the line of prophecy continues in Isa. ix. 6 and Micah v. 3 — so that a further and higher fulfilment in Christ is in no way arbitrary.
1:23:
23. ἡ παρθένος follows the LXX rendering of the Hebrew almah, a more general word later rendered by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion as νεᾶνις (probably, Alford suggests, precisely to avoid the Messianic application, rather than because that application was not already current).

καλέσουσιν — the indefinite plural ('they shall call') marks that this is to be one of His current appellations, not a formal naming by any one person; it suits a fulfilment of the prophecy wider and more final than the literal one in Isaiah's own day.

Ἐμμανουήλ = 'God with us' — in Isaiah primarily prophetic of deliverance from the contemporary threat of war, but ultimately of the final and glorious deliverance wrought by God manifest in the flesh.

ὅ ἐστιν μεθερμηνευόμενον — this explanatory addition has been used (inconclusively) to argue that Matthew's Gospel was composed in Greek rather than Hebrew, since such a gloss would scarcely be needed in a Hebrew original (see Prolegomena).
1:24: 24. ἐγερθεὶς... ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕπνου — from the sleep in which he had received the dream; παρέλαβεν τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ — he took her formally to his home as his wife, in obedience to the angel's command.
1:25:
25. Bengel's classic comment well states the grammatical force: 'non cognovit eam, donec...' does not of itself imply the contrary afterward; it only certifies her virginity up to the birth, leaving what follows to the fair-minded reader's judgment.

On the much-disputed sense of the verse, Alford observes: (1) the reader's first, natural impression is certainly that the ἐγίνωσκεν was confined to the period here named; (2) nothing elsewhere in Scripture removes that impression — the unqualified phrase 'brethren of the Lord' (cf. ch. xiii. 55) shews the idea was not felt to be repugnant, and the N.T.'s uniformly honourable language about marriage, together with the angel's own words to Joseph, if anything support rather than discountenance the natural reading; (3) the idiom of the verse itself does not require the opposite view. In Alford's judgment no one would ever have read the verse otherwise than in its plain sense except to force it into agreement with a preconceived doctrine of the perpetual virginity of Mary — a view whose great historical champion, tellingly, was Jerome, himself the great impugner of marriage as such (see Milman, Hist. of Latin Christianity, i. 72 ff.).

ἐκάλεσεν — i.e. Joseph (see ver. 21), exercising the father's right and duty of naming the child.
2:1:
vv. 1–12. Visit and Adoration of the Magi. 1. Βηθλεὲμ τῆς Ἰουδαίας distinguishes it from the other Bethlehem in Zebulun (Josh. xix. 15); 'Bethlehem-Judah' (Judg. xvii. 7–9; 1 Sam. xvii. 12), also called Ephrath or Ephrata, six Roman miles south of Jerusalem, known as 'the city of David.'

ἐν ἡμέραις Ἡρώδου — Herod the Great, son of the Idumean Antipater, made king of Judæa at Rome and confirmed after Actium; a reign marked by cruelty (he put to death his wife Mariamne and his own sons Alexander, Aristobulus, and finally Antipater) alongside great public works, including the rebuilding of the Temple. He died at seventy, in the thirty-eighth year of his reign. The events here narrated occurred shortly before his death.

μάγοι ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν — 'the East' may denote Arabia, Persia, Chaldæa, or Parthia; in all of these there were practitioners of the wider 'magian' arts. Both Suetonius and Tacitus attest a widespread Eastern persuasion, about this very time, that out of Judæa a world-ruler would arise — likely fed by Balaam's prophecy (Num. xxiv. 17) and by Daniel's seventy weeks (Dan. ix. 24), which an astrologically-minded East could plausibly have known. There is no ancient ground for the later tradition that the magi were three in number or were kings — the 'three' arose from the number of the gifts, the 'kings' from Isa. lx. 3 and Ps. lxxii. 10.
2:2:
2. αὐτοῦ τὸν ἀστέρα — Alford devotes an extended (and, by his own account in his day, controversial) note to whether the star was a miraculous appearance or a natural phenomenon providentially used and providentially interpreted. He inclines, on the evidence of the magi's own language ('we have seen his star,' the language of astrological observation) and of Rev. C. Pritchard's astronomical calculations, to a remarkable triple conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in Pisces in 747 A.U.C. — a conjunction which, on the chronology of the magi's journey, would indeed have stood in the appropriate quarter of the sky both at the outset and on the approach to Bethlehem. He is emphatic that this in no way denies the miraculous character of the *guidance*, only locates the sign within ordinary astronomical appearances, citing Wetstein's remark that God may make use of men's own arts and errors (as with Joseph's brethren, or the Babylonian king's divination in Ezek. xxi. 21) to bring about His purposes.

ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ — not 'at its rising' but 'in the East,' i.e. either the eastern country they came from, or the eastern sky.

προσκυνῆσαι — to do homage in the Eastern manner of prostration before a king.
2:3: 3. ἐταράχθη... πᾶσα Ἱεροσόλυμα — Herod, a foreign usurper, feared a rival claimant to the throne; the populace, exhausted by years of sedition and slaughter under him, feared fresh tumults — and there may also be an echo of the popular belief that Messiah's coming would be preceded by great tribulations (cf. the Rabbinic Sohar, cited by Schöttgen).
2:4: 4. συναγαγὼν πάντας τοὺς ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ γραμματεῖς — i.e., as Lightfoot explains, he assembled the Sanhedrim: under ἀρχιερεῖς are comprised the priests and Levites of the seventy-one-member council (the High Priest, his kin, and any who had held the office), under γραμματεῖς the teachers and interpreters of the Law — though usually the πρεσβύτεροι τοῦ λαοῦ are named as a third class alongside these two (cf. ch. xvi. 21; xxvi. 3, 59); possibly on this occasion, the question being purely one of scriptural learning, only the priests and scribes were summoned.
2:6:
5, 6. καὶ σύ, Βηθλεέμ — a free paraphrase, not exact citation, of Micah v. 2 — the Sanhedrim's own answer to Herod, but adopted by the Evangelist as substantially correct.

γῆ Ἰούδα — γῆ need not stand for πόλις; the district, not merely the town, may be meant (cf. ver. 16).

ἡγεμόσιν renders the Hebrew word for the military 'chiliads' or clan-divisions into which the tribes were organized, each inscribed in the public registers of its city — hence 'thou art not least among the *captains* (clan-heads) of Judah,' rather than, as in Micah's own wording, 'thousands.'

ἐκ σοῦ γὰρ ἐξελεύσεται ἡγούμενος — it has even been suggested that the curious Latin phrase found in both Tacitus and Suetonius, that world-rulers would come 'profecti Judaea,' echoes this very LXX wording.
2:7: 7. ἠκρίβωσεν — ascertained with precision; τὸν χρόνον τοῦ φαινομένου ἀστέρος — the time (duration) of the star's appearing, reckoned from when the magi first saw it — the position of the participle excludes the rendering 'the time when the star appeared' as a single point.
2:8: 8. πορευθέντες... ἐξετάσατε ἀκριβῶς — the pleonastic doubling (πορευθέντες... ἐλθὼν προσκυνήσω) is a familiar Hebraism, also natural enough in English, lending fulness without being strictly necessary to the sense.
2:9: 9. ἐπάνω οὗ ἦν τὸ παιδίον — may mean simply 'over that part of Bethlehem' rather than directly over a particular house; Alford cautions against pressing the description into requiring a strictly miraculous, localized hovering, noting that Scripture commonly uses popular astronomical language, and it is the spirit rather than the letter of the narrative that should govern our reading here (cf. note on ver. 2).
2:11:
11. μετὰ Μαρίας — no significance should be read into the omission of Joseph here (he is named in the parallel visit of the shepherds, Luke ii. 16); it is best taken as simply recording that Joseph happened not to be present, which itself speaks for the narrative's plain truthfulness.

τὴν οἰκίαν — if pressed (as Alford thinks it should be), this implies the family was by this time lodged in a house rather than the stable of Luke's nativity narrative, consistent with some interval having elapsed since the birth; Alford discusses at length, without insisting on a firm answer, how the magi's visit fits with Luke's chronology of the Purification, and emphasizes that apparent tensions between two honest, independent narratives are exactly what we should expect, and are themselves a mark of authenticity rather than of contradiction.

θησαυρούς — chests or bales for carrying treasure on a journey; the gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh were given patristic symbolic readings (gold for a king, myrrh for one who would die, frankincense for God) from very early — already in Irenaeus and Origen.
2:13:
vv. 13–23. The Flight into Egypt, the Massacre of the Innocents, and the Return. 13. ἐγερθεὶς παράλαβε — 'arise and take,' not 'when thou hast arisen, take': the command was for immediate execution, as νυκτός below confirms — Joseph departed that same night. Egypt was near, was a Roman province independent of Herod's jurisdiction, and had a large Jewish population, making it an easy and natural refuge.

τοῦ ἀπολέσαι — a genuine Greek (not Hebraistic) construction expressing purpose, increasingly common from Xenophon and Demosthenes onward.
2:15: 15. ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐκάλεσα τὸν υἱόν μου (Hosea xi. 1) — written originally of Israel as God's son coming up out of Egypt (cf. Exod. iv. 22, 23), and applied here under the standard N.T. principle that the whole typical economy of Israel finds its true and final referent in the Messiah. The ἵνα of purpose must be taken seriously and not explained away as merely marking result.
2:16: 16. Josephus records no such slaughter, but the silence is unsurprising given how small an incident this would have been amid the bloodshed of Herod's last years and how small a town Bethlehem was. Josephus himself testifies that 'a black bile, raging beyond all his other passions, possessed him' (Antt. xvii. 6. 5); Herod had already murdered his wife and three sons. Alford suggests the secrecy implied by λάθρα in ver. 7 indicates Herod intended this very stratagem from the start, preferring a sure, undivulged stroke to an open enquiry that might let the child escape.
2:18: 17, 18. φωνὴ ἐν Ῥαμᾷ ἠκούσθη (Jer. xxxi. 15) — an accommodation, not a literal fulfilment, of a prophecy originally written of the Babylonian captivity; none of its details should be pressed literally. The link is probably Rachel's tomb, traditionally located on the road to Bethlehem (Gen. xxxv. 19), the inhabitants of the district thus poetically reckoned as her 'children' through the long-standing close association of Judah and Benjamin (Ramah itself lying some six miles north of Jerusalem, in Benjamin's territory).
2:19: See 2:13 for the parallel construction; Herod the Great died at Jericho in his seventieth year, the thirty-eighth of his reign (Jos. B.J. i. 33. 8).
2:20: 20. τεθνήκασιν γάρ — the plural is probably not mere idiom or delicacy about the dead, but an echo of Exod. iv. 19 (spoken to Moses in almost identical terms), or, as Meyer suggests, denotes the category of Herod's enemies rather than their literal number.
2:22:
22. Ἀρχέλαος βασιλεύει — Archelaus, son of Herod by the Samaritan Malthace, succeeded to Idumæa, Judæa, and Samaria but held only the title of Ethnarch, not King (the rest of Herod's territory passing to his brothers Philip and Antipas); yet popular usage at the start of his reign did treat him as a king (cf. similarly ch. xiv. 9, of Antipas), explaining the Evangelist's term. In his ninth year Archelaus was deposed for cruelty to both Jews and Samaritans and banished to Vienne in Gaul (Jos. Antt. xvii. 13. 2).

ἀνεχώρησεν εἰς τὰ μέρη τῆς Γαλιλαίας — Alford candidly judges, against attempts (e.g. by Wordsworth) to force ἀνεχώρησεν to mean 'returned,' that read on its own terms Matthew's narrative gives every appearance of having been written without knowledge of Luke's infancy narrative, under the impression that Bethlehem, not Nazareth, was the family's original home — while stressing that, properly understood, the two independent and truthful accounts are not actually inconsistent, only incomplete in different places.
2:23: 23. Ναζωραῖος κληθήσεται — no O.T. text contains these words verbatim, nor does the Evangelist claim one does, only that this is the *sense* of 'the prophets' (plural). Alford surveys four proposed explanations without fully endorsing any: (1) Euthymius and others supposed the precise saying had simply been lost from now-vanished prophetic writings; (2) that the prophets generally foretold Messiah's contempt, as Nazareth was despised (cf. John i. 46) — which Alford finds too general, since Nazareth itself is nowhere shown to have been an object of contempt as such; (3) that it alludes to the Nazirite consecration of men like Samson and Samuel — which Alford rejects, since our Lord did not keep the Nazirite vow (cf. ch. xi. 18, 19) and the Greek spelling of 'Nazirite' differs from 'Nazarene' throughout the N.T.; (4) that it plays on nēṣer, 'Branch' (Isa. xi. 1), the probable root of the place-name itself — the view of various Hebraists, though the standard 'Branch' prophecies (Zech. iii. 8; vi. 12; Jer. xxiii. 5; xxxiii. 15) actually use a different Hebrew word. He leaves the question, finally, an unsolved difficulty.
